hints: Think about why a peak appears at m/e = 107, one unit above the molecular ion, and which naturally occurring isotope present at about 1.1% abundance causes it.
walkthrough:
See where the M+1 peak comes from**
You have $M$ at $m/e = 106$ and a small $M+1$ at $m/e = 107$ that is 8% of the height of $M$. That extra mass is almost entirely due to molecules containing one $^{13}\text{C}$ atom instead of $^{12}\text{C}$. Each carbon atom contributes about 1.1% to the size of the $M+1$ peak.

Do the simple division**
Use $$n = \frac{\text{abundance of M+1}}{1.1} = \frac{8}{1.1} \approx 7.3$$ You cannot have 0.3 of an atom, so you round to the nearest whole number, giving $n = 7$ carbon atoms in F.
Final answer: Abundance of M+1 relative to M = n x 1.1%, so n = 8 / 1.1 = 7.3, therefore 7 C atoms per molecule of F.

hints: Use your result from (i) that the molecule is rich in carbon, and try to fit mass 91 using 7 carbons plus hydrogens, remembering the fragment must carry a + charge.
walkthrough:
Build mass 91 from carbon and hydrogen**
G has $M_r = 212$ and contains phenyl groups, so a hydrocarbon fragment is likely. Try $7 \times 12 = 84$ for seven carbons. That leaves $91 - 84 = 7$ for hydrogens, giving $\text{C}_7\text{H}_7$.

Add the charge and recognise the ion**
In the mass spectrometer the fragment is a cation, so write $\text{C}_7\text{H}_7^+$. This is the very stable benzyl / tropylium ion, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2^+$, which is why it gives a major peak.

hints: Start with Mr of F = 106 containing 7 carbons and oxygen, and work out what combination of H and O gives the correct mass.
For G, use Mr = 212 and the clue that two molecules of F combine to make G, thinking about what small molecule is typically lost when an ester forms.
walkthrough:
Find the formula of F**
Seven carbons contribute $7 \times 12 = 84$ to the mass. $M_r$ of F is 106, so $106 - 84 = 22$ remains for H plus O. With one oxygen ($16$), that leaves $6$ for hydrogen. So F is $\text{C}_7\text{H}_6\text{O}$. Check: $84 + 6 + 16 = 106$.

Find the formula of G**
Two molecules of F would be $2 \times \text{C}_7\text{H}_6\text{O} = \text{C}_{14}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2$. Its mass is $2 \times 106 = 212$, which exactly matches the molecular ion of G at $m/e = 212$. So no atoms are lost here, G is $\text{C}_{14}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2$.

Final answer: F is $\text{C}_7\text{H}_6\text{O}$
G is $\text{C}_{14}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2$

hints: Combine the formula C7H6O with the 1H NMR singlet at delta 10.0 for one proton to identify the functional group in F.
Use the hydrolysis products benzoic acid plus phenylmethanol to work backwards to the ester linkage present in G.
walkthrough:
Pin down F as benzaldehyde**
$\text{C}_7\text{H}_6\text{O}$ with a phenyl ring ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$) leaves $\text{CHO}$. The $^1\text{H}$ NMR singlet at $\delta$ 10.0 for $1\text{H}$ is classic for an aldehydic proton, $\text{R-CHO}$. So F is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$, benzaldehyde.

Pin down G as the ester**
Heating G with dilute acid gives $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ + $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. That pair of acid plus alcohol comes from an ester. Join them with loss of water: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO-O-CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$. This is benzyl benzoate. It fits $\text{C}_{14}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2$, fits fragments $m/e = 105$ ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}^+$) and $m/e = 91$ ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_7^+$), and fits formation from two benzaldehydes.

Final answer: F is benzaldehyde, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$
G is benzyl benzoate, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOCH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$

hints: Recall which proton in benzaldehyde is highly deshielded near delta 10, and which protons in benzyl benzoate sit next to oxygen near delta 5.
walkthrough:
Match shift to environment**
In F, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$, the proton attached directly to $\text{C=O}$ is strongly deshielded and appears as a $1\text{H}$ singlet at $\delta$ 10.0, so circle that aldehydic H. In G, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOCH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$, the two equivalent protons on the carbon attached to oxygen, $\text{-O-CH}_2\text{-}$, appear as a $2\text{H}$ singlet at $\delta$ 5.1, so circle that $\text{CH}_2$ group.
Final answer: On F circle the aldehydic H of $\text{CHO}$ ($\delta$ 10.0). On G circle the $\text{CH}_2$ protons of $\text{OCH}_2$ ($\delta$ 5.1).

hints: Think about the general name for splitting an ester back into carboxylic acid and alcohol using aqueous acid and heat.
walkthrough:
Name the splitting by water**
G, an ester, reacts with water in the presence of dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to give acid plus alcohol: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOCH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$ Breaking a molecule with water is hydrolysis, here acid hydrolysis of an ester.

hints: Order the three compounds by acidity, remembering carboxylic acids are much stronger acids than phenols, which are stronger than alcohols.
Compare the anions formed from 4-methylphenol and phenylmethanol, focusing on what happens to the lone pair on oxygen in each case.
Think about how the extra oxygen in the carboxylate group helps to spread the negative charge compared with a phenoxide ion.
walkthrough:
State the acidity order**
Acid strength increases with stability of the conjugate base. The order is benzoic acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, strongest, then 4-methylphenol, $\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{OH}$, then phenylmethanol, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, weakest.

Explain phenol versus alcohol**
When 4-methylphenol loses $\text{H}^+$, it forms $\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{O}^-$. The lone pair on oxygen can overlap with the pi system of the ring, so the negative charge is delocalised over the ring. When phenylmethanol loses $\text{H}^+$, it forms $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$. The $\text{CH}_2$ group breaks conjugation, so the charge stays localised on oxygen. Delocalisation stabilises the phenoxide, making the phenol more willing to release $\text{H}^+$.

Explain why benzoic acid is strongest**
The benzoate anion, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2^-$, has the negative charge delocalised equally over two highly electronegative oxygen atoms through the $\text{C=O}$ group. This electron withdrawing carbonyl provides extra stabilisation compared with a single phenoxide oxygen, so benzoic acid dissociates most readily.

Final answer: Acidity: benzoic acid > 4-methylphenol > phenylmethanol.
4-methylphenol is more acidic than phenylmethanol because the lone pair on the phenoxide O is delocalised into the benzene ring, stabilising the anion, whereas the negative charge in $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$ is localised on O.
Benzoic acid is strongest because its anion is further stabilised by delocalisation over two electronegative O atoms / electron withdrawing $\text{C=O}$ group.

hints: Recall why direct esterification of a phenol with a carboxylic acid is poor, and what more reactive derivative of benzoic acid you should make first.
Identify the reagent that converts CO2H into COCl and draw the structure of the intermediate formed.
Think about how to make the phenol act as a better nucleophile in step 2 before it reacts with the acyl chloride.
walkthrough:
Activate benzoic acid as the acyl chloride**
Phenols are poor nucleophiles, so heating benzoic acid directly with 4-methylphenol gives very low yield. Make the much more reactive benzoyl chloride first: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl} + \text{SO}_2 + \text{HCl}$$ The intermediate is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$. $\text{PCl}_5$ works equally well.

Generate the phenoxide nucleophile**
Dissolve 4-methylphenol in $\text{NaOH(aq)}$: $$\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{OH} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ The phenoxide ion is a much stronger nucleophile than the neutral phenol.

Form the phenyl ester**
Shake the alkaline phenoxide solution with benzoyl chloride at room temperature. Nucleophilic acyl substitution gives the ester: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl} + \text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{O}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{OCOC}_6\text{H}_5 + \text{Cl}^-$$ This is 4-methylphenyl benzoate.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$ (intermediate benzoyl chloride). $\text{PCl}_5$ is an alternative.
Step 2: dissolve 4-methylphenol in $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ to form phenoxide, then shake with $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$ at room temperature to give 4-methylphenyl benzoate.
